scenario.title: Lakeside Water — billing dispute surge (Mock #6, not an official contest problem)
scenario.description: Billing dispute tickets roughly doubled in August-September. Customer Service wants an AI agent. Field reading is contracted out; AMI meters and the meter data management system (MDMS) are run by a vendor.
scenario.initial_request: Dispute tickets doubled since August. Build an AI agent that auto-answers billing dispute tickets and fixes whatever is causing the wrong bills.

potential_bias: frames the issue as a response-speed problem

H-FIELD-READ-FAILURE.statement: Contracted field‑meter reading routes or staffing have deteriorated since August, leading to missed manual reads, estimate substitution, and wrong bills.

interpretation_history.interpretation: Dispute volume rose from ~600 tickets in June/July to ~1,180–1,260 tickets in August/September, indicating roughly double the pre‑August level.
Manual meter‑read completion in August‑September was 88% (9,200 accounts) against a 95% target, indicating a shortfall in field reads that could lead to estimate substitution and disputed bills.

The CRM dispute ticket response times are within the SLA, with a median of 1.6 days and a 90th percentile of 2.8 days against a 3‑day SLA, while handling 2,440 tickets. This indicates the team is meeting response targets despite the high dispute volume.
The observation shows more disputed bills arise from actual reads (1,785) than from estimated reads (1,240), indicating that the dispute surge is not solely driven by estimate substitution.
The tariff change log contains no records, indicating no tariff changes were made in the billing system during the observed period.

interpretation_history.interpretation: The service contract confirms that route priority changes can be requested by the utility but must be executed after Field Operations Manager confirmation, aligning with the existing K-DISPATCH requirement for runtime approval.

framing_assertion.rationale: The initial request states dispute tickets doubled since August and seeks an AI agent to address the underlying cause.

hypotheses.statement: Dispute volume increase is the primary problem; an AI agent that auto-answers tickets and fixes unknown bill errors will restore baseline.
hypotheses.rationale: If true, the solution focuses on ticket deflection and generic bill‑fixing rather than a specific root cause.

hypotheses.statement: AMI read deliveries to MDMS have degraded since August, causing missing reads, estimate substitution, and incorrect bills.
hypotheses.rationale: If true, fixing the AMI‑to‑MDMS pipeline (or improving read completeness) would directly reduce wrong bills, making an AI answer‑agent less critical.

hypotheses.statement: Contracted field‑meter reading routes or staffing have deteriorated since August, leading to missed manual reads, estimate substitution, and wrong bills.
hypotheses.rationale: If true, improving field‑read execution (route adherence, staffing) would address the bill error source, shifting focus away from an AI ticket‑answering agent.

hypotheses.statement: A recent change to billing import validation rules (since August) introduced logic that mis‑classifies or mis‑calculates charges, generating erroneous bills.
hypotheses.rationale: If true, reverting or correcting the rule set would eliminate the bill errors, making an AI answer‑agent a secondary mitigation.

hypotheses.statement: The estimation/substitution algorithm used when no accepted read is available has a defect that produces systematically incorrect bills since August.
hypotheses.rationale: If true, patching the estimation logic would correct bill accuracy; the AI agent would still be useful for ticket handling but not the primary fix.
